rounds.text: Rajputana Biodiesel Ltd trades at an attractive P/E ratio of 17x while delivering exceptional historical growth, featuring a 5-year compounded sales growth of 66% and a 5-year compounded profit growth of 53% [E1, E8, E11]. This impressive performance is underscored by a robust ROCE of 22.0% and an ROE of 20.0%, outperforming the sector median ROCE of 10.5% [E6, E7, E63]. Furthermore, a discounted cash flow analysis indicates an intrinsic value of Rs 634 per share against a market price of ₹ 218, presenting a substantial margin of safety of 65.6% [E2, E32, E33]. The business is actively scaling its operations, having successfully enhanced capacity at its Phulera and Meerut units by almost 3-4 times, with management aiming to produce 130 to 150 kilolitres per day from the coming financial year [E64, E69]. Growth is further supported by structural expansion into compressed biogas and biomass pellets alongside long-term supply contracts with oil marketing companies like HPCL, BPCL, and IOCL [E71, E77]. Conceded: operating cash flow for March 2026 was negative at Rs -3 Cr, free cash flow stood at Rs -15 Cr, and borrowings increased to Rs 28 Cr [E22, E23, E26].

Conceded: [E6]. Despite the reported historical return metrics, Rajputana Biodiesel Ltd exhibits severe cash flow distress as operating cash flow dropped to negative ₹ 3 Cr and free cash flow plummeted to negative ₹ 15 Cr in March 2026 [E22, E23]. This yields an alarming cash conversion ratio of -0.27x against reported profit, indicating that accounting gains are failing to materialize as actual cash [E21]. Meanwhile, financial leverage is expanding rapidly with borrowings doubling from ₹ 14 Cr to ₹ 28 Cr year-over-year [E26]. Operational efficiency is also deteriorating, evidenced by operating margins declining steadily over the last four years and contracting further to 11% in March 2026 [E17, E18, E19]. Institutional confidence has evaporated entirely, with foreign and domestic institutional holdings slashed to 0.01% and 2.65% respectively amid negative institutional money flow [E29, E30, E31]. Finally, the equity lags severely behind the broader market with a relative strength rating of 15 and a price sitting below both its 50-day and 200-day moving averages [E37, E38].

Conceded: [E22, E23]. The negative cash flow and rising borrowings to ₹ 28 Cr [E26] are direct results of a massive capital expenditure build-up, highlighted by a 700% surge in capital work-in-progress to ₹ 8 Cr [E27] to fund 3-4x capacity enhancements at Phulera and Meerut [E69]. This deliberate growth spend supports surging revenue trajectories, including a 66% 5-year and 81% trailing twelve-month sales growth [E8, E10], while debtor days have healthily improved from 72 to 46.8 days [E47]. While the bear highlights margin compression [E17, E18, E19], this reflects a heavy transition phase as the company enters high-margin compressed biogas (CBG) and biomass pellets segments [E71], where management notes potential EBITDA margins exceed 55% to 60% [E73]. Institutional departures [E29, E30] and lagging price momentum [E37, E38] simply represent stale sentiment ignoring fundamental tailwinds, as the company is producing record-high OMC supply bids [E76], completing ₹ 100 crore allocations [E75], and targeting 130 to 150 kilolitres per day from April [E64] within a strong chemicals sector tailwind [E60].

Conceded: [E8, E10]. The bull attributes negative operating cash flow [E22], negative free cash flow of Rs -15 Cr [E23], and surging borrowings doubling to Rs 28 Cr [E26] merely to a growth spend, but ignoring these capital drain metrics as a temporary transition phase overlooks actual financial deterioration. The claim that capital expenditure explains the cash burn fails to justify why operating cash flow collapsed to negative 6% of operating profit [E24] with a cash conversion of -0.27x [E21]. Furthermore, dismissing margin compression as a byproduct of entering new segments ignores that yearly operating margins have suffered a four-year declining trend [E19] and dropped to 11% in Mar 2026 [E18]. While the bull points to capacity plans [E64] and institutional outflows as stale sentiment [E29, E30], the resulting negative money flow signal [E31], price lagging below both the 50-day and 200-day moving averages [E37], and a relative-strength rating of just 15 [E38] reflect tangible market skepticism toward these unverified high-margin projections. Finally, citing large-scale OMC orders [E68] does not excuse a complete 0.00% dividend yield [E4] for shareholders while debt actively compounds.

Conceded: [E21, E22, E23, E24, E26]. The bear characterizes cash burn and rising borrowings as pure financial deterioration, but overlooks that capital expenditures and CWIP surging +700.0% to Rs 8 Cr directly represent active growth spending and technical upgrades [E27, E79]. The four-year margin trend [E19] and recent reading of 11% [E18] accompany a massive 81% trailing twelve-month sales growth surge [E10] and 52% profit growth [E13], proving that scale is intentionally being prioritized over short-term margin retention. While the bear flags institutional outflows [E29, E30] and technical weakness below the moving averages [E37], results scoring 79/100 and a 33% year-over-year net profit jump demonstrate that sentiment and price action lag behind fundamental operating performance [E52, E59]. Furthermore, citing a 0.00% dividend yield [E4] ignores management's explicitly stated strategic roadmap to deploy capital into immediate working capital needs, technical upgrades, capacity enhancements, and balance sheet deleveraging rather than cash distributions [E79, E80].

Conceded: [E27]. The bull argues that negative cash flow and soaring debt are merely symptoms of growth and capital expenditure, yet operating cash flow collapsed to negative ₹3 Cr and free cash flow plunged to negative ₹15 Cr in Mar 2026 [E22, E23], meaning the business is burning cash at an alarming rate that far outpaces normal reinvestment. While the bull claims scale is being prioritized over short-term margin retention, operating margins have experienced a persistent, four-year downward trend, falling to 11% in the latest quarter against 16% in the year-ago period [E18, E19]. The suggestion that price action and institutional sentiment are simply lagging behind strong fundamentals is refuted by the massive institutional exodus, with foreign and domestic institutional holdings crashing by 3.39 and 8.18 percentage points respectively, signaling a profound lack of sophisticated confidence [E29, E30]. Finally, dismissing the zero dividend yield [E4] as part of a deleveraging and growth roadmap [E79, E80] rings hollow when borrowings have simultaneously doubled from ₹14 Cr to ₹28 Cr in a single year [E26].
